replying_to: Replying to Residual Contrastive Learning: Unsupervised Representation Learning from Residuals
display_title: Official Review of Paper2926 by Reviewer wMFe

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes to train an encoder-decoder network for low-level vision tasks, e.g., image denoising.  
The contribution of the paper is to link image denoising with contrastive learning. The assumption is that the noise distribution between two crops sampled from the same image is on average smaller than those sampled from different images. Based on this assumption, a contrastive learning framework is set up in terms of image residuals (rather than image features).  
Experiments on synthetic and real noisy data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed pretraining scheme.
content.main_review:
Strength:
- It is a novel and insightful idea to incorporate image residuals (instead of image features) into the contrastive learning framework. In this sense the connection between image denoising and contrastive learning is established.

Weakness:
- In Table 1, MoCo v2 performs significantly worse than other methods. The reason, however, is unclear. The setting in Table 1 is a linear evaluation setting, where the pretrained weights are fixed. MoCo v2 is the only method that pretrains the encoder only, and it thus has more randomly initialized parameters to be fine-tuned in the following stage. Is the inferior performance of MoCo v2 due to the pretext task misalignment or that MoCo v2 does not train the decoder? The authors are recommended to add the following experiments to make the conclusion more convincing.
    - Some existing papers pretrain dense image features using contrastive learning for dense image recognition tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation. These methods pretrain both the encoder and decoder, but the pretext task misaligns with low-level vision (as claimed in the submission). Comparing with them might make things clearer. Examples include [a] and [b].
    - [a] Pedro O. Pinheiro, Amjad Almahairi, Ryan Y. Benmalek, Florian Golemo, Aaron Courville. Unsupervised Learning of Dense Visual Representations. In NeurIPS, 2020.
    - [b] Zhenda Xie, Yutong Lin, Zheng Zhang, Yue Cao, Stephen Lin, Han Hu. Propagate Yourself: Exploring Pixel-Level Consistency for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning. In CVPR, 2021.
- The perceptual loss in Eq. (9) relies on a pretrained ResNet-50 on ImageNet using labeled data. This setting makes the proposed approach no longer an `unsupervised` learning approach, in the strict sense. A more serious issue is that when comparing the proposed method to existing self-supervised methods (e.g., in Table 1), it is unclear whether the performance gain comes from the proposed design, or the pretrained weights of ResNet-50. I have the following suggestions to mitigate this issue.
    - Can $g_e$ in Eq. (9) be removed? I mean, comparing the pixel loss instead of the perceptual loss.
    - Can $g_e$ be instantiated with the pretrained weights using MoCo v2 on ImageNet?
- Most of the experiments are conducted on synthetic data, except for the last line of Section 4 that shows quantitatively the effectiveness of the proposed method on real noisy datasets. It would be better to add more results on real noisy data, because the noise distribution of synthetic data follows exactly the assumption in the paper (but it is not always true in the real world). Some suggestions to the authors are listed as follows.
    - What is the performance of other self-supervised learning methods on the SIDD dataset?
    - Leaderboard of the SIDD dataset can be found at https://www.eecs.yorku.ca/~kamel/sidd/benchmark.php. The supervised learning result in this paper is far from the state-of-the-art. I am not familiar with this subdivided area. Are there any related methods that need to be mentioned?
- The paper is not easy to read. Many revisions can be made to make it easier to understand.
    - After reading the first page, I know that the proposed approach is not a general pretraining method but aims to solve low-level vision problems. It would be nice to clarify it in the title.
    - Section 3.3, Page 4: "a normalized first-order tensor". To be simple, "a normalized vector" is recommended.
    - The LHS of Eq. (5) is $L_{contrast}$, but $L_{contrastive}$ appears in the RHS of Eq. (10).
    - It would be much better to provide some diagrams or pseudocode of the proposed approach, to make the paper easier to understand.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposes a novel idea to introduce contrastive learning (in terms of image residuals) into the pretraining for low-level vision tasks. The technical part is insightful.  
However, the experiments fail to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. It is arguable whether the performance improvement should be attributed to the proposed method or other issues (e.g., unfair experimental settings and data).  
I hence cannot recommend acceptance.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.

content.title: Clarifications on Experimental Setting
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time, feedback, and suggestions that improve the quality of our work. We are encouraged by the positive comments relating to both the novelty of our ideas and the quality of our ablations and experimental work.from all reviewers, e.g. "**novel**" [wRf6, wMFe], "**good quality**" [wRf6], "**well-written**" [wRf6, Kkbe], "**easy to read**" [wRf6], "**insightful**" [wMFe], "**good ablations and experiments**" [wRf6], "**competitive quantitative results**" [Kkbe].

First, the authors would like to clarify the purpose of experimental design.  
1. The goal of this paper is to present a representation learning framework for low-level vision tasks with noisy inputs, instead of achieving state-of-the-art performance in a single task, such as denoising or super resolution. In fact, one of the contributions of the work is that we utilize the UCL to learn more transferable representations than task-dependent SSL methods. We validate this point using our simulated experiments. 
2. We choose the synthetic data for our main experiments as there exists no such multi-purpose real dataset to validate the transferability of the learned representations. Experiments on the real data provide some initial evidence that the performance achievable on synthetic data should also be feasible on real data.
3. The major contribution is to study the representation learning on noisy inputs. The main baselines are selected for SSL on noisy inputs. Though similar UCL methods have been proposed for high-level vision tasks, but due to task misalignment, they are not suitable for low-level vision tasks.

**Q**: Is the inferior performance of MoCo v2 due to the pretext task misalignment or that MoCo v2 does not train the decoder?   
**A**: Thank you for the question. Please note; the suggested baselines do have task misalignment as they are designed for high-level vision tasks, same as MoCo v2, which are not the problem we aim to address in our work. The purpose of including MoCo v2 is to show that RCL shows obvious advantages over the original UCL. We have included the suggested baselines VADeR and PixContrast [1, 2] in Sections 4.2.1 and 4.2.2 and the same conclusion holds.

[1] Pinheiro, et al.. Unsupervised Learning of Dense Visual Representations. In NeurIPS, 2020.  
[2] Xie, et al.. Propagate Yourself: Exploring Pixel-Level Consistency for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning. In CVPR, 2021.

**Q**:  Can $g_e$ in Eq. (9) be removed? Can g_e be instantiated with the pre-trained weights using MoCo v2 on ImageNet?  
**A**:  The perceptual loss is not necessary, yet we find that using the perceptual loss instead of a pixel loss can lead to a 0.5 dB improvement in PSNR. Thus, we did not include the pixel loss in the initial version. Note, N2N and N2S can not utilize the perceptual loss in such a fashion. Moreover, the pre-trained weights are not necessarily trained in a supervised fashion, as the reviewer suggests. The pre-trained weights just make sure that the noisy inputs and predicted outputs could be measured in the same feature space, as a regularization term. We have included more discussion in Section 3.4.

**Q**: It would be better to add more results on real noisy data.  
**A**:  We have to rely on synthetic data as we aim to understand the transferability of the representations learned by RCL and RCL is not purely designed for denoising. There is no such dataset to the best of our knowledge. The experiments on the real datasets are just to illustrate that similar phenomena are observed in both real and synthetic data.

**Q**: What is the performance of other self-supervised learning methods on the SIDD dataset?  
**A**: The experiments on SIDD are solely included in order to validate that RCL does work on real datasets and can be used to improve the performance of supervised denoising under the same conditions and reduce annotation cost. We do not mean to claim that RCL should be considered the state-of-the-art in denoising. Note, as the goal of universal (multi-purpose) representation learning, there is no such a real dataset that we can leverage. Instead, we have shown that RCL has more advantages over other SSL baselines on the synthetic data. That is to say, previous task-dependent SSL denoising methods learn less transferable representations than RCL. The suggestion to consider alternative methods on SSID might be considered more of an exercise in architecture design. Here the focus is on the learning paradigm, and thus a better comparison would be taking any given network and to see how its performance varies using supervised vs. unsupervised pre-training + fine-tuning, which is the setting we explore. We have expanded Section 4.4 for clarity.

**Q**: Many revisions can be made to make it easier to understand.   
**A**: Thank you for your suggestion. We have revised the manuscript following your suggestions, as described in the Summary of Revision.

replying_to: Replying to Residual Contrastive Learning: Unsupervised Representation Learning from Residuals
display_title: Official Review of Paper2926 by Reviewer Kkbe

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Primary claim: Residual learning has shown success for low-level vision tasks (and high-level vision tasks) in the context of supervised learning. However it has not shown success for low-level vision tasks in the context of self-supervised learning. We provide the first study of contrastive learning for low-level vision tasks and in doing so bridge this gap.

Motivation: As far as I can tell, the full motivation for self-supervised representation learning for the tasks at hand (denoising / super resolution) is "In many cases, y is unavailable due to annotation costs, e.g. obtaining ground truth data for low-level vision tasks typically requires complex and often constraining procedures."

Method: A contrastive loss over residuals n(x) = x - f_learned(x), computed from positive/negative image-crop pairs, is defined in terms either Bhattacharyya distance, Earth mover's distance, or maximum mean discrepancy. f_learned is trained by minimizing this contrastive loss alongside a perceptual loss/consistency loss term for regularization.

Results: Quantitative results are provided using MIT Demosaicing, Stanford Taskonomy, PASCAL VOC, in terms of PSNR and SSIM. Residual contrastive learning is shown to be comparable to N2N and N2S. No qualitative results are provided, despite end goals of denoising / super resolution / demosaicing.

Claimed Contributions: 1. First formulation of instance-wise pretext task based on residuals (and adaptation of InfoNCE to do so). 2. Proposal of residual contrastive learning + the first study of CL for low-level vision tasks; 3. Demonstration that RCL can learn robust representations without paired ground truth.
content.main_review:
The primary strengths are that the paper is written clearly when it comes to details and that the proposed method attains competitive quantitative results (in terms of PSNR and SSIM) for denoising and super resolution.

One weakness is the lack of motivation: the motivation in the introduction should be much stronger. For example, why should the reader care about 'unsupervised contrastive learning' for the tasks considered in the paper (denoising, demosaicing, super resolution), when obtaining pairs for supervision is often simple (as done in much of the prior cited work)? If this is indeed difficult, then please provide examples.

Another weakness is that the method is largely a combination of existing ideas. This is not necessary a weakness if combined with very strong empirical results + discussion, but that is not the case here.

Another weakness is the limited results. There are few quantitative results, little discussion, and no qualitative results at all, which is especially alarming since the tasks in the paper are denoising / super resolution / demosaicing. Example: As a distance measure between probability distributions, the authors consider Bhattacharyya distance, Earth mover's distance, and maximum mean discrepancy, and in Table 1 show that EMD leads to marginally better PSNR and SSIM. The full discussion surrounding this is "RCL with EMD shows robust performance in comparison to RCL with both BD and MMD and may thus be preferred in practical denoising applications." In addition, given the goals, qualitative results in the form of random visualizations (noisy, clean pairs) are a must.

Small details:

Right after equation 2, please fix "n ~ P(n)", or omit it entirely if the only aim is to say that n is a random variable.

Assumption 1: This statement seems obvious (and has already been exploited in many papers). Is it for some reason not obvious, such that highlighting it in such a pronounced way makes sense? There is no "Assumption 2" anywhere, correct?
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper offers a combination of existing techniques to build residual contrastive learning, which aims to leverage self-supervised learning for low-level vision tasks such as denoising and super resolution. As such, it is purely an empirical paper. Given this, the paper should provide a proper motivation of why this is important along with a strong array of results that suggest that the proposed approach is promising. Instead, the paper does not properly motivate the approach, and with regard to results, provides only a limited set of quantitative results, with no qualitative results at all, and with little discussion/insight. Therefore I can't recommend its acceptance.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.

content.title: Clarification of Contributions
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time, feedback, and suggestions that improve the quality of our work. We are encouraged by the positive comments relating to both the novelty of our ideas and the quality of our ablations and experimental work.from all reviewers, e.g. "**novel**" [wRf6, wMFe], "**good quality**" [wRf6], "**well-written**" [wRf6, Kkbe], "**easy to read**" [wRf6], "**insightful**" [wMFe], "**good ablations and experiments**" [wRf6], "**competitive quantitative results**" [Kkbe].


Firstly we would like to highlight our contributions, which are threefold:
1. We propose residual contrastive learning, **the first unsupervised residual learning framework**.   
2. We **adapt unsupervised contrastive learning (UCL) to low-level vision tasks with noisy inputs** by building a link between UCL and residual learning.  
3. We provide empirical evidence towards evidencing our claim that **representations learned by RCL are more transferable than previous SSL methods for noisy inputs**. **significantly reduce annotation cost**, and **RCL does not suffer from task alignment**.


**Q**: The motivation in the introduction should be much stronger.  
**A**: Thank you for your suggestion. We highlight that label scarcity does exist in the real world. Even though datasets with "noise-free" labels might exist in the denoising literature, we argue it is valuable to have an unsupervised learnable representation that can naturally be robust to noisy input data, as all image data is deemed to be affected by a certain amount of noise. To the best of our knowledge, those GT labels are rarely provided in a number of tasks that use noisy images input data. UCL learns more transferable representations than other SSL methods in high-level vision tasks. We aim to utilize this property in low-level vision representation learning. We have further strengthened these points in our introduction in the revision.


**Q**: The method is largely a combination of existing ideas.    
**A**: We would respectfully disagree with this. To the best of our knowledge, both the use of residuals as the discriminative feature for UCL and exploring UCL for low-level vision tasks with noisy inputs are novel ideas and constitute previously unexplored directions. 


**Q**: No qualitative results.    
**A**: We politely emphasize that **the qualitative comparison is less meaningful** in this work. The primary target of this work is representation learning, which learns representations for downstream tasks instead of directly solving the problems. We follow [1,2], and adopt a **proxy evaluation protocol** to evaluate the quality of the representations. Note, the representations of the intermediate layers are fixed. To assess the intermediate representations, we use the fine-tuned last layer to indirectly reflect the quality of fixed representations. This evaluation protocol is **different from the commonly seen protocols in low-level vision tasks**, where the end-to-end solutions can be compared directly, without fine-tuning, either numerically or visually. Note, the reported numbers only represent the **proxy** / relative performance. It is worth mentioning that the visual difference for proxy evaluation between N2N, N2S, and RCL is negligible for human eyes. As the qualitative results do not directly reflect the performance of representation learning, we choose to omit the visualizations in the main paper. We have clarified this in Section 4.1.3 in the revision.   

[1] He, et al.. Momentum contrast for unsupervised visual representation learning. CVPR 2020   
[2] Chen, et al.. A simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. ICML 2020  


**Q**: Limited results.  
**A**:  We politely emphasize that we are exploring a new research area. There are limited previous studies in this field.  The goal of our experiments is to illustrate that the representations learned by RCL have more transferability than other task-dependent SSL methods on noisy inputs (e.g. N2N, N2S). Meanwhile, due to the current lack of real-world, multi-task low-level vision datasets, we have to rely on simulated experiments. In the revision, we have included two strong pixel-level baselines VADeR and PixContrast in Section 4.2.


**Q**: Choice of distance metrics.   
**A**: Thank you for the suggestions. Limited by the 9 pages limit, we are unable to include all detailed analyses in the initial submission.  Meanwhile, we want to clarify that the main contribution of this work is the RCL framework, and in-depth analysis of the choice of distance was outside of the initial scope of the paper. We select to use EMD over both BD and MMD based simply on our empirical results and reformulate our language to reflect this. In the revision, we have added more discussion on the choice of distance metrics in Sections 4.2.2, 4.2.3, and 4.2.4.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an instance-wise discrimination pretext task using image residuals. The method uses a contrastive loss function. Also, the paper proposes a framework based on residual contrastive loss. This framework can learn transferable representations from only noisy inputs. The presented results on various downstream tasks show that the framework can produce good results.
content.main_review:
The overall quality of the paper is good and it is fairly easy to follow the main ideas. However, there is not enough intuition provided on why this idea would be good.
The paper provides good ablations and experiments on several down-stream tasks.
There are only a few other methods that this work is compared against in the experiment part. Aren't there any newer state of the art works that are suitable for comparison?
Give more details about the used reconstruction metrics in order for the work to be self-contained.
The experiments and results from chapter 4.4 seem valuable, but there are hard to follow and should be better explained.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, to the best of my knowledge the paper introduce a novel idea: using the residuals in a self-supervised scenario. They provide results on several down-stream tasks. Also the paper is fairly well written.

content.title: Thank you for concrete suggestions.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time, feedback, and suggestions that improve the quality of our work. We are encouraged by the positive comments relating to both the novelty of our ideas and the quality of our ablations and experimental work.from all reviewers, e.g. "**novel**" [wRf6, wMFe], "**good quality**" [wRf6], "**well-written**" [wRf6, Kkbe], "**easy to read**" [wRf6], "**insightful**" [wMFe], "**good ablations and experiments**" [wRf6], "**competitive quantitative results**" [Kkbe].


**Q**: Additional intuition that motivates the potential of the ideas.  
**A**: We thank the reviewer for the suggestion and have strengthened the motivation in the abstract of Section 1, in the revision, accordingly. We note that that contrastive learning (CL) has proven to provide powerful tools for high-level vision tasks, especially **in learning transferable representations**. Intuitively, successful adaptation of such tools, to low-level vision tasks with noisy inputs, provides a straightforward and yet promising direction. Note, noisy inputs are quite common in the real world while **existing representation learning studies only focus on clean inputs**. Accordingly, we define a goal of constructing a CL framework with the capability of addressing low-level vision tasks with noisy input. We achieve this by building a connection between CL and residual learning. 

**Q**: Newer state-of-the-art works that are suitable for comparison?  
**A**: Thank you for the suggestion. We highlight that only **limited relevant related works**; for SSL on noisy inputs exist. Most of the state-of-the-art CL methods are designed for **either high-level vision tasks or clean images**. Our comparisons attempt to **demonstrate that RCL can learn more transferable representations than seminal SSL on noisy inputs and show advantages in mitigating the task misalignment, in contrast to commonly seen CL methods**. We have included VADeR and PixContrast [1, 2] as two further strong pixel-level CL baselines in Section 4.2.1 and Section 4.2.2 in the revision. All CL baselines (MoCo, VADeR, and PixContrast) show severe task misalignment phenomena in the experiments.

[1] Pinheiro, et al.. Unsupervised Learning of Dense Visual Representations. In NeurIPS, 2020.  
[2] Xie, et al.. Propagate Yourself: Exploring Pixel-Level Consistency for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning. In CVPR, 2021.

**Q**: More details about the used reconstruction metrics.  
**A**: Thank you for your suggestion. We have added details pertaining to PSNR and SSIM in the revision, towards helping manuscript self-containment, in Section 4.1.4 in the revision.

**Q**: Section 4.4 is hard to follow and should be better explained.  
**A**: Thank you for your suggestion. We have improved clarity and generally expanded Section 4.4 with further details.

content.title: Summary of Revision
content.comment:
1. We update the title to highlight that the inputs are **noisy images**, as suggested by Reviewer wMFe.


2. We revise the abstract and introduction to highlight the motivation and contribution, as suggested by Reviewer wRf6 and Reviewer Kkbe. Specifically, **we aim to utilize contrastive learning to learn transferable representations**.


3. We include the pseudo-code for *residual contrastive loss* in Algorithm 1, as suggested by Reviewer wMFe.


4. We highlight that the pre-trained encoder could be learned from the noisy inputs directly in Section 3.4, as suggested by Reviewer wMFe.


5. We clarify the experimental setups in Section 4.1, suggested by Reviewer Kkbe and Reviewer wMFe:  
* We clarify the reason for using synthetic data in Section 4.1.1.  
* We clarify the reason for using proxy evaluation in Section 4.1.3. Especially, we highlight **why qualitative visualizations are less meaningful** for this work.


6. We include the details of PSNR and SSIM in Section 4.1.4, as suggested by Reviewer wRf6. 


7. We include additional experimental results, including two state-of-the-art pixel-level contrastive learning baselines [a, b] in Section 4.2.1 and 4.2.2, as suggested by  Reviewer wMFe and Reviewer Kkbe.  
[a] Pinheiro, et al.. Unsupervised Learning of Dense Visual Representations. In NeurIPS, 2020.  
[b] Xie, et al.. Propagate Yourself: Exploring Pixel-Level Consistency for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning. In CVPR, 2021.


8. We add more discussion on the choice of distance metrics, suggested by Reviewer Kkbe. We clarify that the choice of distance metrics is not the focus of this work and is based on empirical results in Sections 4.2.2, 4.2.3, and 4.2.4.


9. We rewrite and expand Section 4.4, as suggested by Reviewer wMFe.
* We clarify the experimental setup and the purpose of the experimental design.
* We include more discussion on the results.


The authors will keep this summary open and updated until the end of the discussion period.
